topics.name: Battle of San Juan Hill
topics.kicker: The Rough Riders’ 1898 charge in Cuba · Made Theodore Roosevelt a hero
topics.briefing: On July 1, 1898, American soldiers charged up a ridge of hills outside Santiago, Cuba, straight into fire from Spanish rifles. Theodore Roosevelt led his volunteer Rough Riders up nearby Kettle Hill beside the Black troopers known as Buffalo Soldiers, then joined the attack on San Juan Hill. The victory trapped Spain’s army and fleet at Santiago and made Roosevelt so famous that New York elected him governor that fall.
topics.answerHtml: Battle of San Juan Hill (or Battle of San Juan Heights; prompt on Kettle Hill; do not accept “Spanish-American War”)
accept: battle of the san juan heights

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: During this battle, an Army Signal Corps observation balloon was towed along a jungle trail above the advancing soldiers. The balloon gave away the Americans’ position to Spanish riflemen, and many soldiers were hit while crowded together at a river crossing below it.
tossups.r: Theodore Roosevelt’s Rough Riders also fought in this battle. For 10 points, name this July 1, 1898, battle outside Santiago, Cuba.

tossups.p: Soldiers named one hill in this battle for a huge iron sugar-making pot that they found on its top. Black cavalrymen of the 9th and 10th Cavalry, nicknamed Buffalo Soldiers, helped capture that hill before joining the attack on a ridge topped by a Spanish blockhouse.
tossups.r: Theodore Roosevelt’s Rough Riders charged up that first hill. For 10 points, name this 1898 battle near Santiago, Cuba.

tossups.p: Lieutenant John Parker earned the nickname “Gatling Gun” Parker after his detachment of hand-cranked rapid-fire guns raked the Spanish trenches during this battle. That covering fire helped American infantry under Jacob Kent climb to a blockhouse at the top of the main ridge.
tossups.r: Theodore Roosevelt’s Rough Riders fought nearby. For 10 points, name this 1898 battle fought outside Santiago, Cuba.

tossups.p: Frederic Remington painted soldiers in this battle charging forward on foot behind a lone officer on horseback. That officer had resigned as Assistant Secretary of the Navy to help raise a volunteer regiment for this battle’s war.
tossups.r: That regiment was the Rough Riders. For 10 points, name this battle that made Theodore Roosevelt a national hero.

tossups.p: In 2001, President Bill Clinton gave a posthumous Medal of Honor for this battle to a man who had been turned down soon after it was fought, possibly because he had angered the War Department by signing a letter urging that sick soldiers be brought home.
tossups.r: That man had led the Rough Riders up Kettle Hill. For 10 points, name this battle that made Theodore Roosevelt a hero.

tossups.p: Days before this battle, General William Shafter’s Fifth Army Corps landed at Daiquirí [“dye-kee-REE”], and a cavalry division under the former Confederate general Joseph Wheeler won a skirmish at Las Guásimas [“GWAH-see-mahs”]. Shafter then ordered this attack on the heights guarding the city of Santiago.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this July 1, 1898, battle in which Theodore Roosevelt led the Rough Riders up Kettle Hill.

tossups.p: John J. Pershing, who later commanded American forces in World War I, fought in this battle as an officer of the 10th Cavalry. That regiment and the 9th Cavalry, Black units nicknamed Buffalo Soldiers, helped capture Kettle Hill during this battle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1898 battle near Santiago, Cuba, where Theodore Roosevelt led the Rough Riders.

tossups.p: During this battle, one officer rode his horse, Little Texas, partway up a slope until a wire fence forced him to continue on foot. That officer’s regiment of cowboys, college athletes, and Native Americans had trained in San Antonio, Texas.
tossups.r: That regiment was the Rough Riders. For 10 points, name this battle of the Spanish-American War that made Theodore Roosevelt famous.

tossups.p: Spanish General Arsenio Linares [“lee-NAH-rays”] was wounded in this battle, whose outnumbered Spanish defenders fired Mauser rifles that used smokeless powder. Many American volunteers carried older rifles, and their clouds of black-powder smoke gave away their positions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this July 1, 1898, battle in Cuba where the Rough Riders charged alongside the Buffalo Soldiers.

tossups.p: The humorist Finley Peter Dunne had his character Mr. Dooley joke that one officer’s memoir of this battle’s campaign should have been titled _Alone in Cuba_, because the author wrote so much about himself.
tossups.r: That 1899 memoir was Theodore Roosevelt’s _The Rough Riders_. For 10 points, name this 1898 battle in which Roosevelt led a famous charge.

tossups.p: On the same day as this battle, Henry Lawton’s division needed hours to capture the nearby village of El Caney [“kah-NAY”], where the Spanish general Joaquín Vara del Rey was killed. Lawton had been expected to take that village quickly and then join this attack on the heights east of Santiago.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this July 1, 1898, battle in Cuba in which Theodore Roosevelt led the Rough Riders.

tossups.p: One man honored for his actions in this battle and his oldest son, honored for leading troops ashore at Utah Beach on D-Day, are one of only two father-and-son pairs to receive the Medal of Honor. The other pair is Arthur and Douglas MacArthur.
tossups.r: The father had led the Rough Riders. For 10 points, name this 1898 battle in which Theodore Roosevelt charged up Kettle Hill.

tossups.p: Glowing newspaper reports by the correspondent Richard Harding Davis helped make one volunteer officer the best-known American hero of this battle. That officer was elected governor of New York about four months later.
tossups.r: He had led the Rough Riders up Kettle Hill. For 10 points, name this 1898 battle in Cuba that made Theodore Roosevelt a national hero.

tossups.p: Shortly before this battle, Colonel Leonard Wood was promoted to lead a brigade, leaving his second-in-command in charge of their regiment, officially the 1st U.S. Volunteer Cavalry. Most of that regiment fought on foot, because there had been no room on the ships for most of their horses.
tossups.r: That regiment was the Rough Riders. For 10 points, name this battle near Santiago, Cuba, where Theodore Roosevelt led a charge.

tossups.p: Two days after this battle, Admiral Pascual Cervera’s Spanish fleet tried to escape from Santiago Harbor and was destroyed by American warships. This battle had given the Americans high ground overlooking that city, which surrendered on July 17.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this July 1, 1898, battle of the Spanish-American War, where Theodore Roosevelt’s Rough Riders charged.

clues.t: Theodore Roosevelt’s volunteer cavalry regiment, the Rough Riders, made a famous charge here
An American victory over Spain in the Spanish-American War (1898)
Fought on July 1, 1898, on the heights just east of Santiago, Cuba
The Rough Riders actually charged up nearby Kettle Hill first, then joined the attack on the main ridge
The 9th and 10th Cavalry, Black regiments nicknamed Buffalo Soldiers, fought beside the Rough Riders
Lieutenant John Parker’s Gatling guns gave covering fire (“Gatling Gun” Parker)
Frederic Remington painted the charge: soldiers on foot behind a lone officer on horseback
Roosevelt got the Medal of Honor for it in 2001 (from Bill Clinton), the only president ever to receive it
The Rough Riders (officially the 1st U.S. Volunteer Cavalry) fought on foot; most of their horses stayed behind in Florida
Made Roosevelt a national hero; New York elected him governor about four months later
Led to the siege of Santiago: Cervera’s fleet was destroyed trying to escape (July 3), and the city surrendered July 17
Kettle Hill was named for a huge iron pot used in making sugar, found on its top
An Army Signal Corps observation balloon above the troops gave away their position to Spanish riflemen
General William Shafter’s Fifth Army Corps had landed at Daiquirí days earlier
Former Confederate general Joseph Wheeler’s cavalry won a skirmish at Las Guásimas a week earlier (June 24)
Jacob Kent’s infantry division stormed the main ridge, which was topped by a Spanish blockhouse
Spanish general Arsenio Linares was wounded; his outnumbered men had Mauser rifles with smokeless powder
John J. Pershing, later the U.S. commander in World War I, fought here with the 10th Cavalry
Roosevelt rode his horse, Little Texas, up the slope until a wire fence stopped him
Leonard Wood was promoted to lead a brigade, leaving Roosevelt in command; the regiment had trained in San Antonio
Mr. Dooley (Finley Peter Dunne) joked that Roosevelt’s memoir _The Rough Riders_ (1899) should be called _Alone in Cuba_
Same day: Henry Lawton’s men took the village of El Caney, where Spain’s General Vara del Rey was killed
Roosevelt and his son Ted Jr. (Utah Beach, D-Day) are one of two father-son Medal of Honor pairs; the MacArthurs are the other
Roosevelt was turned down for the medal at the time, possibly for angering the War Department with a letter urging that sick troops be sent home
Correspondent Richard Harding Davis’s glowing reports helped make Roosevelt the battle’s best-known hero

trap.title: Kettle Hill or San Juan?
trap.body: The Rough Riders’ famous charge was really up Kettle Hill, a smaller hill nearby, before they joined the attack on San Juan Hill itself, so Kettle Hill clues often appear in tossups on this battle. Two other fights get mixed in: Henry Lawton’s attack on El Caney the same day, and the naval Battle of Santiago de Cuba two days later, when Admiral Cervera’s fleet was destroyed. “Spanish-American War” names the whole war, not this battle.
trap.fix: If the question says “this battle” and mentions July 1, 1898, the Rough Riders, the Buffalo Soldiers, or Gatling guns, answer San Juan Hill. Kettle Hill was part of the same attack (the Battle of the San Juan Heights), so it earns only a prompt; El Caney means Lawton’s village fight, and Cervera’s ships mean the July 3 sea battle.
trap.line: Real answer line: Battle of San Juan Hill (or Battle of San Juan Heights; prompt on Kettle Hill)

topics.name: Battle of Shiloh
topics.kicker: Grant’s costly 1862 win in Tennessee · Its huge losses shocked the nation
topics.briefing: Early on April 6, 1862, Confederate troops burst out of the woods near a little log church in southwestern Tennessee and caught Ulysses S. Grant’s army by surprise. Their commander, Albert Sidney Johnston, was killed that afternoon, and the next day Union reinforcements helped Grant drive the Confederates away. With nearly 24,000 men killed, wounded, captured, or missing, Shiloh was the bloodiest battle in American history up to that time.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The Welsh-born journalist Henry Morton Stanley, who later tracked down the missionary David Livingstone in Africa, fought for the Confederacy in this battle and was taken prisoner. The Union soldier Ambrose Bierce later wrote a vivid memoir essay about what he saw in this battle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this April 1862 battle in Tennessee, where Albert Sidney Johnston’s army surprised Ulysses S. Grant’s.

tossups.p: After this battle, Henry Halleck took personal command in the field and moved so slowly toward Corinth, Mississippi, that the Confederates simply abandoned the town in late May. Meanwhile, newspapers blamed the general who had won this battle for letting his army be caught by surprise.
tossups.r: That general was Ulysses S. Grant. For 10 points, name this April 1862 battle in Tennessee.

tossups.p: In a Ray Bradbury short story, a general comforts a frightened young drummer named Joby on the night before this battle. Herman Melville wrote a short requiem for this battle’s dead, describing swallows that skim low over its “forest-field.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this April 1862 battle in Tennessee, where Confederate general Albert Sidney Johnston was killed.

tossups.p: Daniel Ruggles gathered dozens of Confederate cannons to pound a stubborn Union position during this battle. Union troops had held that position, nicknamed the “Hornet’s Nest” for the buzzing of bullets, until Benjamin Prentiss surrendered more than 2,000 men there late in the day.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this April 1862 battle in Tennessee, a hard-won victory for Ulysses S. Grant.

tossups.p: When this battle began, the Union commander was at his headquarters in Savannah, Tennessee, several miles downriver, and he rushed to the fighting by steamboat. A patrol sent out by Benjamin Prentiss had run into the Confederate army just before dawn.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this April 1862 battle, where Albert Sidney Johnston’s Confederates surprised Ulysses S. Grant’s army.

tossups.p: One commander in this battle was shot in the leg near a peach orchard and died within an hour, making him the highest-ranking officer on either side killed in the Civil War. His second-in-command, P. G. T. Beauregard [“BOH-ruh-gard”], called off the attack at nightfall.
tossups.r: That commander was Albert Sidney Johnston. For 10 points, name this April 1862 battle in Tennessee.

tossups.p: A Union division under Lew Wallace marched on the wrong road during the first day of this battle and arrived only as night fell, angering the commanding general. Wallace later became famous as the author of the novel _Ben-Hur_.
tossups.r: Reinforcements under Don Carlos Buell also began arriving that evening. For 10 points, name this battle that Ulysses S. Grant won on April 7, 1862.

tossups.p: In his memoirs, the winning general of this battle wrote that afterward he “gave up all idea of saving the Union except by complete conquest.” On the rainy night after its first day, that general told William Tecumseh Sherman, “Lick ’em tomorrow, though.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this April 1862 battle in Tennessee, won by Ulysses S. Grant.

tossups.p: During the night after this battle’s first day, the Union gunboats _Tyler_ and _Lexington_ fired shells toward the Confederate lines to keep the enemy from resting. By then, the Union army had been pushed back to a steamboat landing on the Tennessee River.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this April 1862 battle, where Ulysses S. Grant’s army was surprised by Albert Sidney Johnston.

tossups.p: John Wesley Powell, who later led a famous boat expedition through the Grand Canyon, lost his right arm while commanding artillery in this battle. In this battle, Union troops held out for hours along a sunken road before they were surrounded.
tossups.r: That position was nicknamed the Hornet’s Nest. For 10 points, name this April 1862 battle in Tennessee won by Ulysses S. Grant.

tossups.p: Before this battle, Confederate forces gathered at the railroad junction of Corinth, Mississippi, after losing Forts Henry and Donelson earlier that year. They marched north from Corinth to strike the enemy before Don Carlos Buell’s army could arrive.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in which Albert Sidney Johnston was killed while attacking Ulysses S. Grant’s army in April 1862.

tossups.p: After this battle, Abraham Lincoln supposedly defended its winning general against critics by saying, “I can’t spare this man; he fights.” This battle’s nearly 24,000 casualties made it the bloodiest battle in American history up to that time.
tossups.r: That general was Ulysses S. Grant. For 10 points, name this April 1862 battle in Tennessee.

tossups.p: Shelby Foote, later known for his storytelling in Ken Burns’s documentary _The Civil War_, wrote a 1952 novel named for this battle. Southerners named this battle for a small log church whose Hebrew name is often translated as “place of peace.”
tossups.r: Northerners named it for a nearby steamboat landing. For 10 points, name this April 1862 battle in Tennessee.

tossups.p: On the first morning of this battle, William Tecumseh Sherman’s division was caught by surprise near a log church, and Sherman was wounded in the hand. Sherman had dismissed warnings that a large Confederate army was nearby.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this April 1862 battle where Confederates under Albert Sidney Johnston surprised Ulysses S. Grant’s army.

tossups.p: On the second day of this battle, fresh troops from Don Carlos Buell’s Army of the Ohio joined a Union counterattack that drove the Confederates back toward Corinth. The night before, P. G. T. Beauregard [“BOH-ruh-gard”] had sent a message to Richmond claiming a complete victory.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this April 1862 battle in Tennessee, where Ulysses S. Grant’s army recovered from a surprise attack.

clues.t: Fought April 6–7, 1862, in southwestern Tennessee, beside the Tennessee River
Ulysses S. Grant’s Union army was surprised on the first day but won on the second
Confederate commander Albert Sidney Johnston was killed, the highest-ranking officer on either side killed in the war
Southerners named it for a log church (a Hebrew name often translated “place of peace”); Northerners named it for a steamboat landing
Union troops held the “Hornet’s Nest” along a sunken road for hours, until Benjamin Prentiss surrendered more than 2,000 men
P. G. T. Beauregard took over after Johnston died and halted the attack at nightfall
Don Carlos Buell’s Army of the Ohio arrived that evening and overnight, and helped Grant win on April 7
Nearly 24,000 casualties: the bloodiest battle in American history up to that time
William Tecumseh Sherman’s division was surprised near the church; Sherman was wounded in the hand
The Confederates marched from the railroad junction of Corinth, Mississippi, and retreated there afterward
Lew Wallace’s division took the wrong road and arrived as night fell; Wallace later wrote the novel _Ben-Hur_
On the rainy first night, Grant told Sherman, “Lick ’em tomorrow, though”
Grant’s memoirs: afterward he “gave up all idea of saving the Union except by complete conquest”
Johnston was shot in the leg near a peach orchard and died within an hour
The Union gunboats _Tyler_ and _Lexington_ fired shells toward the Confederate lines through the night
Daniel Ruggles gathered dozens of Confederate cannons to pound the Hornet’s Nest
Grant was at his headquarters in Savannah, Tennessee, when it began; a patrol from Prentiss’s division found the Confederates before dawn
Afterward, Henry Halleck took command and crept toward Corinth, which the Confederates abandoned in late May 1862
Lincoln supposedly defended Grant afterward: “I can’t spare this man; he fights”
Henry Morton Stanley, who later found David Livingstone in Africa, fought for the Confederacy and was captured
Union soldier Ambrose Bierce later wrote a memoir essay about what he saw there
John Wesley Powell, later famous for exploring the Grand Canyon by boat, lost his right arm there
Ray Bradbury’s short story about a young drummer named Joby takes place the night before it
Herman Melville wrote a requiem poem for its dead (swallows over the “forest-field”); Shelby Foote wrote a 1952 novel about it

trap.title: Same names, different battles
trap.body: Shiloh had a Sunken Road and a Peach Orchard, but so did other famous battles: Antietam’s Sunken Road became “Bloody Lane,” and Gettysburg had its own Peach Orchard. Shiloh also gets mixed up with Ulysses S. Grant’s other Western victories, Fort Donelson (February 1862), where he demanded “unconditional surrender,” and the Siege of Vicksburg (1863). The two sides even used different names for this battle.
trap.fix: Listen for April 1862, Tennessee, a log church, the Hornet’s Nest, Albert Sidney Johnston’s death, Beauregard, Buell, and Lew Wallace. Both names, Shiloh (the Southern name, after the church) and Pittsburg Landing (the Northern name, after the steamboat landing), are correct.
trap.line: Real answer line: Battle of Shiloh (or Battle of Pittsburg Landing)

topics.name: Battle of Trenton
topics.kicker: Washington’s Christmas-night surprise · Revived the American cause
topics.briefing: On Christmas night in 1776, George Washington’s ragged army rowed across the ice-choked Delaware River in a freezing storm, then marched nine miles through sleet and snow. On the morning of December 26, they surprised about 1,500 Hessian soldiers at Trenton, New Jersey, and captured nearly 900 of them in less than an hour. After months of defeats, the victory gave the American Revolution new life.
topics.answerHtml: Battle of Trenton (prompt on crossing of the Delaware; do not accept “Princeton”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: On the night before this battle, John Glover’s regiment of Marblehead fishermen ferried troops in big flat-bottomed Durham boats, which had been built to carry iron ore. Henry Knox’s booming voice helped direct that crossing through a storm of sleet and snow.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this December 26, 1776, battle in which George Washington surprised Hessian soldiers in New Jersey.

tossups.p: The army that won this battle set out from McConkey’s Ferry in Pennsylvania. It landed at Johnson’s Ferry, New Jersey, about three hours behind schedule, and then began a nine-mile march through a storm.
tossups.r: The ferry site is now called Washington Crossing. For 10 points, name this battle won after George Washington crossed the Delaware River on Christmas night, 1776.

tossups.p: About two weeks before this battle, British cavalry captured the American general Charles Lee at a tavern in Basking Ridge, New Jersey. By then, the American army had lost New York City and retreated across New Jersey, and many soldiers’ enlistments would run out at the end of the year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this morale-boosting battle in which George Washington’s army crossed the Delaware and surprised the Hessians.

tossups.p: In this battle, Nathanael Greene’s division struck from the north along the Pennington Road while John Sullivan’s division advanced along the River Road. When Sullivan sent word that his men’s muskets were too wet to fire, their commander supposedly replied that they should use the bayonet.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this December 1776 battle in which George Washington surprised Hessian soldiers in New Jersey.

tossups.p: Colonel Johann Rall [“RAHL”] was mortally wounded in this battle while trying to rally his three regiments, which came from the German state of Hesse-Kassel. Nearly 900 of his soldiers were captured in less than an hour.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle that George Washington won the morning after crossing the Delaware River on Christmas night, 1776.

tossups.p: Shortly before this battle, its winning commander had his soldiers hear a new essay warning that “the summer soldier and the sunshine patriot” would shrink from serving their country. The password for the night march before this battle was “Victory or Death.”
tossups.r: That essay was Thomas Paine’s _The American Crisis_. For 10 points, name this battle where George Washington surprised the Hessians in December 1776.

tossups.p: Captain William Washington and Lieutenant James Monroe were both wounded in this battle while leading a charge that captured two enemy cannons on King Street. Monroe, a future president, is traditionally said to hold the flag in a famous painting of the crossing before this battle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this December 26, 1776, battle in which George Washington defeated the Hessians.

tossups.p: A week after this battle, Charles Cornwallis was held off at Assunpink Creek and supposedly boasted that he would “bag” the “old fox” in the morning. His enemy slipped away overnight, leaving campfires burning, and won at Princeton on January 3, 1777.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this December 1776 battle in New Jersey, where George Washington captured hundreds of Hessians.

tossups.p: Emanuel Leutze [“LOYT-suh”] painted the river crossing before this battle while living in Düsseldorf, Germany, and he mistakenly showed a Stars and Stripes flag that was not adopted until 1777. His painting of that crossing hangs in New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this December 26, 1776, battle that followed George Washington’s crossing of the Delaware River.

tossups.p: New Jersey’s 1999 state quarter, labeled “Crossroads of the Revolution,” shows the river crossing that led to this battle. This battle and a victory at Princeton about a week later formed the heart of the “Ten Crucial Days.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in which George Washington surprised Hessian soldiers on December 26, 1776.

tossups.p: Two American soldiers died from the cold during the night march before this battle, as a nor’easter pelted the army with sleet and snow. Some of the marchers had no shoes and wrapped their feet in rags.
tossups.r: Their commander, George Washington, had crossed the Delaware River on Christmas night. For 10 points, name this 1776 battle in New Jersey.

tossups.p: After this battle, the winning army recrossed the river into Pennsylvania that same day, bringing nearly 900 prisoners along with captured muskets and cannons. Those prisoners were German soldiers whose ruler had rented them to the British army.
tossups.r: They were called Hessians. For 10 points, name this battle that George Washington won on December 26, 1776.

tossups.p: General Hugh Mercer was mortally wounded at a battle fought about a week after this one, and the Americans then went into winter quarters at Morristown, New Jersey. In this earlier battle, about 2,400 Americans attacked at around eight in the morning after a night march of about nine miles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in which George Washington surprised the Hessians the morning after Christmas, 1776.

tossups.p: Alexander Hamilton, then a young captain, commanded a company of New York artillery in this battle. Henry Knox placed cannons at the head of the town’s two main streets, King and Queen Streets, which fired down on enemy soldiers as they tried to form ranks.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in which George Washington defeated Hessian soldiers in New Jersey in December 1776.

tossups.p: Because ice kept James Ewing’s militia from crossing the river to seize a bridge, several hundred enemy soldiers escaped across Assunpink Creek during this battle. John Cadwalader’s planned crossing farther south also failed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in which George Washington captured nearly 900 Hessians after crossing the Delaware on Christmas night, 1776.

clues.t: George Washington crossed the icy Delaware River on Christmas night 1776 to launch this attack
Surprised and captured Hessians, German soldiers hired by the British
Fought December 26, 1776, in a New Jersey town that is now the state capital
A small battle but a huge morale boost after months of American defeats
The Hessian commander, Colonel Johann Rall, was mortally wounded
The Americans’ password for the night march was “Victory or Death”
Washington had Thomas Paine’s _The American Crisis_ (“These are the times that try men’s souls”) read to his troops beforehand
Emanuel Leutze’s 1851 painting shows the crossing; James Monroe is traditionally said to hold the flag
About a week later, Washington won again at Princeton (January 3, 1777)
John Glover’s regiment of Marblehead fishermen rowed the boats across the river
Nearly 900 Hessians were captured in less than an hour; only a handful of Americans were wounded
James Monroe and William Washington were wounded leading a charge that captured two Hessian cannons
Henry Knox directed the crossing with his booming voice and aimed cannons down King and Queen Streets
The troops crossed in Durham boats, big flat-bottomed boats built to haul iron ore
They crossed from McConkey’s Ferry, Pennsylvania (now Washington Crossing), to Johnson’s Ferry, New Jersey, about three hours late
Ice stopped two other crossings, by James Ewing and John Cadwalader, so some Hessians escaped over Assunpink Creek
Two columns attacked: Nathanael Greene’s on the Pennington Road and John Sullivan’s on the River Road; Washington supposedly told Sullivan to “use the bayonet”
A nor’easter brought sleet and snow; two Americans died from the cold on the march
Captain Alexander Hamilton commanded a company of New York artillery
About two weeks earlier, British cavalry captured General Charles Lee at a tavern in Basking Ridge, New Jersey
A week later, Cornwallis was held off at Assunpink Creek and supposedly planned to “bag” the “old fox,” but Washington slipped away, leaving campfires burning
The heart of the “Ten Crucial Days” (December 25, 1776–January 3, 1777)
General Hugh Mercer was mortally wounded at Princeton; the army then wintered at Morristown
New Jersey’s 1999 state quarter (“Crossroads of the Revolution”) shows the crossing
Leutze painted it in Düsseldorf, Germany; its Stars and Stripes flag is a mistake (adopted 1777); it hangs in the Metropolitan Museum of Art

trap.title: Trenton or Princeton?
trap.body: George Washington won two surprise victories in New Jersey about a week apart: Trenton on December 26, 1776, where he captured Hessians after crossing the Delaware, and Princeton on January 3, 1777, where he beat British troops after slipping away from Cornwallis. In between came a second fight at Trenton, at Assunpink Creek on January 2. The password “Victory or Death” can trick you too: William Travis signed his famous 1836 letter from the Alamo with the same words.
trap.fix: Christmas night, the Delaware crossing, Hessians, Johann Rall, and Durham boats mean Trenton. Hugh Mercer’s death and campfires left burning to fool Cornwallis mean Princeton. If you only say “crossing the Delaware,” expect a prompt, because the moderator wants the battle.
trap.line: Real answer line: Battle of Trenton (prompt on crossing of the Delaware; do not accept “Princeton”)

topics.name: Cabinet of the United States
topics.kicker: The president’s top advisers · Heads of the executive departments
topics.briefing: The Constitution never uses the word “cabinet.” It says only that the president may require the written opinion of the “principal Officer” in each executive department. George Washington’s first cabinet had just four members, including the bitter rivals Thomas Jefferson and Alexander Hamilton. It has since grown to include the heads of 15 departments, from State and Treasury to Homeland Security, which was created in 2002.
topics.answerHtml: Cabinet of the United States (accept President’s Cabinet or U.S. Cabinet; prompt on executive departments; do not accept “Executive branch,” “Secretary of State,” or “Kitchen Cabinet”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Each year, one member of this group skips the State of the Union address and waits at a secret location as the “designated survivor.” This group’s department heads follow the Speaker and the president pro tempore in the line of succession, in the order their departments were created.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of the president’s top advisers, whose highest-ranking member is the Secretary of State.

tossups.p: Under Section 4 of the 25th Amendment, the vice president and a majority of this group’s department heads can declare that the president is unable to do the job. In 1920, Woodrow Wilson forced out his secretary of state, Robert Lansing, for calling meetings of this group while Wilson was ill.
tossups.r: Its members include the secretaries of State, Treasury, and Defense. For 10 points, name this group of top presidential advisers.

tossups.p: The Constitution never names this body, but Article II lets the president require the written “Opinion” of the “principal Officer” in each executive department. George Washington started the custom of meeting with those officials as a group.
tossups.r: Most of its members are called secretaries. For 10 points, name this group of the president’s top advisers, who lead departments such as State and Treasury.

tossups.p: In 1834, the Senate rejected Roger Taney [“TAW-nee”] as Secretary of the Treasury, the first time it voted down a president’s choice for this group. In 1989, it rejected John Tower’s nomination to join this group as Secretary of Defense.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of presidential advisers, whose members must be confirmed by the Senate.

tossups.p: In 1841, every member of this group except Secretary of State Daniel Webster resigned after John Tyler vetoed bills to create a new national bank. A decade earlier, the Petticoat Affair over Peggy Eaton had broken up Andrew Jackson’s first version of this group.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of top advisers, made up mostly of the heads of the executive departments.

tossups.p: Critics complained that Andrew Jackson ignored his official advisers in favor of a “Kitchen” version of this group, which included the newspaper editors Amos Kendall and Francis Blair. Jackson also gave the Postmaster General a seat in this group, which lasted until the Post Office was reorganized in 1971.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of the president’s top advisers, which includes the Secretary of State and the Attorney General.

tossups.p: In 1953, Oveta Culp Hobby of Houston became the second woman in this group, as the first Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare. Twenty years earlier, Frances Perkins had become the first woman in this group, serving as Franklin Roosevelt’s Secretary of Labor.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of top presidential advisers who lead the executive departments.

tossups.p: In 1966, Robert C. Weaver became the first African American in this group, as the first Secretary of Housing and Urban Development under Lyndon Johnson. In 2001, Colin Powell became the first African American to hold this group’s top-ranking post, Secretary of State.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of the president’s top advisers, whose members lead the executive departments.

tossups.p: Edmund Randolph, who presented the Virginia Plan at the Constitutional Convention, served in the first version of this group as Attorney General. Henry Knox, the namesake of Fort Knox, served alongside him as Secretary of War.
tossups.r: Thomas Jefferson and Alexander Hamilton also served in George Washington’s first version of this group. For 10 points, name this group of presidential advisers.

tossups.p: Two rap “Battles” in the musical _Hamilton_ show Thomas Jefferson and Alexander Hamilton arguing at meetings of this group over Hamilton’s debt plan and over whether to help France. George Washington asked members of this group for written opinions on whether a national bank was constitutional.
tossups.r: Jefferson served in this group as Secretary of State, and Hamilton as Secretary of the Treasury. For 10 points, name this group of top advisers to the president.

tossups.p: The Tenure of Office Act of 1867 required Senate approval before a president could fire certain officials, including members of this group. Andrew Johnson was impeached after he tried to remove one of them, Secretary of War Edwin Stanton, and in 1926 the Supreme Court said that law had been unconstitutional.
tossups.r: Most of its members are called secretaries. For 10 points, name this group of presidential advisers who lead the executive departments.

tossups.p: In 2002, Congress combined 22 agencies into a new department, which became the newest department represented in this group. Tom Ridge was the first person to hold that post, Secretary of Homeland Security.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of top presidential advisers, made up mainly of the heads of 15 executive departments.

tossups.p: Doris Kearns Goodwin’s book _Team of Rivals_ describes how Abraham Lincoln filled this group with men who had run against him for the 1860 nomination, including William Seward and Salmon Chase. Lincoln later made Chase Chief Justice after he left this group.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of top presidential advisers, whose members must be confirmed by the Senate.

tossups.p: The Department of Commerce and Labor, created in 1903, was split into two separate departments in 1913, each with its own seat in this group. The old War Department lost its seat after 1947, when it became part of what was soon renamed the Department of Defense.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of the president’s top advisers, which includes the heads of 15 executive departments.

tossups.p: Among the department heads in this group, only the leader of the Justice Department, which was created in 1870, does not carry the title “Secretary.” Other members of this group include the vice president, and some presidents have added officials such as the ambassador to the United Nations.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this body of top presidential advisers, which first met under George Washington.

clues.t: The president’s group of top advisers, mostly the heads (secretaries) of the executive departments
George Washington’s first one had four members: Jefferson (State), Hamilton (Treasury), Knox (War), and Randolph (Attorney General)
Its members are nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate
Includes the heads of 15 executive departments, plus the vice president and other top officials
Not named in the Constitution; Article II lets the president require the written “Opinion” of the “principal Officer” of each department
Andrew Jackson’s unofficial “Kitchen” advisers, such as editors Amos Kendall and Francis Blair, were nicknamed after it
First woman member: Frances Perkins, Franklin Roosevelt’s Secretary of Labor (1933–1945)
First African American member: Robert C. Weaver, Secretary of Housing and Urban Development under Lyndon Johnson (1966)
Newest department: Homeland Security (2002), formed from 22 agencies after the September 11 attacks; Tom Ridge led it first
Tenure of Office Act (1867): Senate approval needed to fire certain officials; Andrew Johnson was impeached after trying to remove Edwin Stanton
Its department heads follow the vice president, Speaker, and president pro tempore in the line of succession, in the order their departments were created
Jefferson and Hamilton clashed in Washington’s meetings over the national bank, helping start the first political parties
Abraham Lincoln’s “Team of Rivals” included former opponents William Seward and Salmon Chase
One member skips the State of the Union address as the “designated survivor”
25th Amendment, Section 4: the vice president and a majority of its department heads can declare the president unable to serve
Woodrow Wilson forced out Secretary of State Robert Lansing (1920) for calling its meetings while Wilson was ill
The Senate first rejected a nominee in 1834 (Roger Taney for Treasury); it also rejected John Tower for Defense (1989)
In 1841, all of John Tyler’s department heads except Daniel Webster resigned after he vetoed national bank bills
The Petticoat Affair over Peggy Eaton broke up Andrew Jackson’s first one (1831)
The Postmaster General had a seat from Andrew Jackson’s time until 1971, when the Post Office became the U.S. Postal Service
Oveta Culp Hobby of Houston, the first Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare (1953), was the second woman member
Firsts at State: Madeleine Albright, the first woman Secretary of State (1997), and Colin Powell, the first African American (2001)
Fort Knox, Kentucky, is named for the first Secretary of War, Henry Knox; Edmund Randolph had presented the Virginia Plan
Two rap “Battles” in the musical _Hamilton_ show Jefferson and Hamilton arguing at its meetings (the debt plan; whether to help France)
The Tenure of Office Act was repealed in 1887; in 1926 the Supreme Court said it had been unconstitutional
The Attorney General, head of the Justice Department (created 1870), is the only department head not called “Secretary”
Commerce and Labor (1903) split into two departments in 1913; the War Department lost its seat after 1947, when Defense took over

trap.title: A group, not a branch
trap.body: This answer is a group of people, so naming one member (such as the Secretary of State) or the whole executive branch is wrong. Andrew Jackson’s “Kitchen Cabinet” was an unofficial circle of friends and newspaper editors, not the official group, and Franklin Roosevelt’s “Brain Trust” was a team of professors who advised him. Because the Constitution never uses the word “cabinet,” clues about the “principal Officer” of each executive department point here.
trap.fix: If the question says “this group” or “this body” and mentions department heads, secretaries, Senate confirmation, or the line of succession, say “Cabinet.” If it asks only for Jackson’s informal advisers, the answer is the Kitchen Cabinet; if it describes one office, name that office.
trap.line: Real answer line: Cabinet of the United States (accept President’s Cabinet; do not accept “Executive branch” or a single cabinet post)
